question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You control only ONE of your opponent's turns, not two — but that opponent ends up taking two extra turns afterward. You DO get a second Emrakul, the Promised End (as a token copy). And no, copying the spell does NOT give you a second "you gain control of a turn" trigger.

Details:

1) Controlling turns: Emrakul, the Promised End's cast trigger reads "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." When you copy that triggered ability with Lithoform Engine's {2},{T} ability, the copy is put on the stack above the original (707.10, 707.10b) and resolves first. It creates a control effect over your opponent's very next turn (call it Turn 1) plus a delayed trigger promising an extra turn after Turn 1. Then the original trigger resolves and does the same thing: it also tries to grant you control of that opponent's "next turn," which is still Turn 1 (it hasn't started yet). Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, "Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works. If multiple players have cast Emrakul and targeted the same player, each ability's effect will create an extra turn." That means you still only actually control Turn 1 once (the later-created effect just overwrites the earlier one, it doesn't stack into a second controlled turn), but BOTH triggers still separately set up their own "after that turn, take an extra turn" delayed ability. So after Turn 1 ends, your opponent gets two extra turns of their own (not controlled by you), added one at a time per rule 500.7, with the most recently created one taken first. Net result: you control 1 turn, and your opponent then plays 2 extra turns back-to-back before returning to normal turn order.

Note: this assumes you left the copy targeting the same opponent. Lithoform Engine's ability lets you choose a new target for the copy (707.10). In a game with more than two players, you could instead point the copy at a *different* opponent, in which case you'd control each targeted opponent's own next turn (two separate controlled turns, one per player) instead of the overwrite scenario above. With only two players there's only one opponent to target, so this doesn't apply, and this whole answer is for that same-opponent case (whether two-player or multiplayer with the same target chosen).

2) Second Emrakul: Yes. Lithoform Engine's {4},{T} ability copies target permanent spell you control — here, the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack. Per rule 111.13, "A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token." So you'll get a 13/13 flying, trample, protection-from-instants Emrakul, the Promised End token in addition to the original Emrakul, the Promised End once it resolves normally.

3) No extra cast trigger: Emrakul, the Promised End's ability that grants you control of a turn triggers specifically "When you cast this spell." Lithoform Engine ruling #6 states plainly: "The copy is created on the stack, so it's not 'cast' or 'activated.' Creating the copy won't cause abilities that trigger when a player casts a spell or activates an ability to trigger." Since the Lithoform Engine copy of Emrakul, the Promised End is never cast, the cast-triggered "gain control" ability does not trigger again for that copy. (Separately, Lithoform Engine ruling #5 notes that copies of permanent spells can't have new targets chosen if they have any, but that's irrelevant here since the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself has no targets — only its triggered ability does.)

cited_text.500.7: Some effects can give a player extra turns. They do this by adding the turns directly after the specified turn. If a player is given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. If multiple players are given extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time, in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). The most recently created turn will be taken first.
cited_text.111.13: A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token. The token is not “created” for the purposes of any replacement effects or triggered abilities that refer to creating a token.

cited_text.101.4: If multiple players would make choices and/or take actions at the same time, the active player (the player whose turn it is) makes any choices required, then the next player in turn order (usually the player seated to the active player’s left) makes any choices required, followed by the remaining nonactive players in turn order. Then the actions happen simultaneously. This rule is often referred to as the “Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) order” rule. A card reads “Each player sacrifices a creature.” First, the active player chooses a creature they control. Then each of the nonactive players, in turn order, chooses a creature they control. Then all creatures chosen this way are sacrificed simultaneously.

question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
For X=0, casting Awaken the Woods costs {1}{G}{G} (1 generic mana plus two green mana, 3 mana total) and creates 0 Forest Dryad tokens — you'd be paying the full 3-mana floor for nothing. You should instead cast it with X=2: it costs the exact same {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total) but nets you 2 Forest Dryad tokens instead of 0.

Here's the math. Awaken the Woods's mana cost is {X}{G}{G}; per rule [107.3a] and [601.2b], you announce X as part of casting, and that announced value is what determines both the mana you owe and the number of tokens the spell creates (Awaken the Woods's own text: 'Create X 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens'). To find the actual total cost, rule [601.2f] has you take the mana cost, apply cost increases, then cost reductions (the mana component can never drop below {0}), and 'once the total cost is determined... it becomes locked in.' Trinisphere's own ruling [Trinisphere ruling #0] specifies the exact order for it: start with the mana/alternative cost, add cost increases, apply cost reductions, and only then check Trinisphere's 'less than three mana' condition and bump the cost up to three mana if needed (Trinisphere's card text: 'each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast costs three mana to cast,' with the reminder text showing the extra mana gets added as generic mana on top of the existing colored symbols, e.g. {1}{B}→{2}{B}).

Working through each X:
- X=0: mana cost {0}{G}{G}. Your green-cost reducer would take {1} off the generic portion, but it's already {0} and can't go below {0} [601.2f]. So before Trinisphere, the cost is still {0}{G}{G} — only 2 mana total, which is less than three, so Trinisphere raises it to {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total: 1 generic + 2 green). You get 0 tokens.
- X=1: mana cost {1}{G}{G}. The reducer knocks the generic {1} down to {0}. That's again only 2 mana total (2 green), so Trinisphere again bumps it to {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total). You get 1 token — same 3-mana price as X=0, but one token instead of zero.
- X=2: mana cost {2}{G}{G}. The reducer knocks the generic {2} down to {1}. That's {1}{G}{G} = 3 mana total already, so Trinisphere's 'less than three' condition never triggers (no further increase). Final cost is {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total: 1 generic + 2 green) — identical price to X=0 and X=1 — but you get 2 tokens.
- X=3: mana cost {3}{G}{G}. Reducer takes it to {2}{G}{G} = 4 mana total, which is not less than three, so Trinisphere doesn't apply. Cost is {2}{G}{G} (4 mana total) for 3 tokens — now you're paying an extra mana beyond the floor.

So X=0 and X=1 are strictly wasteful: Trinisphere's three-mana floor forces you to pay 3 mana regardless, and your {1} cost reducer only cancels out that floor exactly at X=2. Casting with X=2 gets you the maximum number of tokens for the minimum mana Trinisphere will ever let you pay ({1}{G}{G}, 3 mana total). If you have extra mana to spend beyond that floor, going higher (X=3, X=4, ...) keeps being reasonably efficient (each additional token beyond the floor costs exactly 1 more generic mana, since the reducer keeps knocking 1 off X's generic contribution), but X=2 is the 'free' sweet spot you should choose over X=0 or X=1.

This assumes a standard two-player-style cost calculation; nothing in the rules given ties this to player count, so the same math applies at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

That land becomes a 0/0 Elemental creature with haste. It’s still a land.” Casting a spell using its awaken ability follows the rules for paying alternative costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h.

Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X. If a spell or activated ability has a mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, and/or activation cost with an {X}, [-X], or X in it, and the value of X isn’t defined by the text of that spell or ability, the controller of that spell or ability chooses and announces the value of X as part of casting the spell or activating the ability. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) While a spell is on the stack, any X in its mana cost or in any alternative cost or additional cost it has equals the announced value. While an activated ability is on the stack, any X in its activation cost equals the announced value.

A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.

Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It can’t be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.” If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while it's in your graveyard, but the end result is that Animate Dead falls off and you have to sacrifice Grist. Here's why: per Grist, the Hunger Tide's own text and [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types" — so in the graveyard Grist is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect, which is a valid legal target for Animate Dead's "Enchant creature card in a graveyard" requirement.

When Animate Dead resolves ([Animate Dead ruling #0], [Animate Dead ruling #1]), Grist returns to the battlefield under your control and Animate Dead attaches to it, gaining the ability "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura." But the instant Grist is on the battlefield, its own text says it's no longer a creature — it becomes "just a planeswalker" ([Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]). Since Grist is no longer a creature, it no longer matches Animate Dead's enchant requirement, so Animate Dead can't legally remain attached to it. Per [Animate Dead ruling #4], this means Animate Dead becomes an illegally-attached Aura and is put into your graveyard as a state-based action. That triggers Animate Dead's delayed ability, "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." When that trigger resolves, if Grist is still on the battlefield (which it will be, since nothing else removed it), you must sacrifice it.

Net effect: Grist briefly enters the battlefield as a planeswalker under your control, Animate Dead immediately dies as a state-based action for being illegally attached, and then you sacrifice Grist when the resulting trigger resolves. You get essentially no lasting benefit from returning Grist this way — it comes back only to be sacrificed almost immediately (though you would get to activate a loyalty ability, if you have priority before the sacrifice trigger resolves, since Grist is on the battlefield as a planeswalker with loyalty in the meantime).
